correctness.rationale: Orient from a star's center to its leaves; the admissible outdegrees are exactly H=<k,k+1>. A number qk+r with 0<=r<k is in H exactly when r<=q. If either shore size is in H, put all centers on the opposite shore. Otherwise a<=b<k(k-1), a+b>=k^2-1 implies a>=k+2, and b=qk+r with 1<=q<r. Set T=b(a-k). Then T>=k(k-1), so L=ceil(T/(k+1)) and J=T-kL have 0<=J<=L. The identity aq(k+1)-T=kb-a(r-q)>0 gives L<=aq. Put the L slots into a rows with capacity q each and upgrade J slots. The resulting allowable row sums d_i are <=b and sum to b(a-k). A direct independent realization concatenates intervals of lengths d_i and reduces their column indices modulo b: no row repeats a column and each column is used exactly a-k times. B-shore outdegrees are then k. This also verifies the manuscript's Gale–Ryser step. For a=k-1, b=k(k-1)-1, the vertices of degree k-1 cannot be centers and the other centers would need the forbidden outdegree b, proving sharpness. The frozen script was inspected, not executed. Its 3,221 loop pairs are the cases tested below the conductor under its additional loop bounds; independent counting gives 385 pairs there with neither shore size representable. This distinction does not affect the all-parameter proof.

value.rationale: This is the exact first degree-sum threshold on a natural graph class for Lee's consecutive-size decomposition problem. It is one below the all-k multipartite obstruction. The uniform constructive upper bound handles precisely the cases where neither shore size is representable and cannot be obtained by putting all centers on one side, and the one-below obstruction applies at every k.
